adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The Cedar Hollow reservoir supplies drinking water to roughly ninety thousand households across three counties. Water leaves the reservoir through a screened intake and passes a series of mechanical bar racks that catch branches, leaves and other debris. From there it flows through a sedimentation basin, where fine grit settles to the bottom over several hours. Pumps lift the settled water to the primary filter gallery, a long hall lined with beds of anthracite coal and sand. Each bed is backwashed on a schedule set by the operators, usually every thirty-six to forty-eight hours, depending on turbidity readings taken at the intake.

After filtration the water passes a clearwell, where chlorine is added and fluoride is adjusted to the level recommended by the state health department. The control room holds a wall of monitors that show flow rates, pressure differentials and chemical concentrations in real time. Operators log every reading by hand as well as in the digital system, a redundancy that the district maintains in case the network fails. Alarms sound when a pump overheats, when a filter bed clogs faster than expected, or when the chlorine residual drifts outside its permitted band.

A maintenance crew of six keeps the pumps, valves and blowers in working order. Their workshop occupies the north end of the gallery and smells of grease and cut steel. Spare impellers, gaskets and motor windings fill shelves that reach the ceiling, each bin labeled with a part number and a purchase date. A separate archival log, kept since the plant opened in 1962, records every structural change to the site. In the spring of 1998, a small survey team entered the lower chamber to map the original drainage lines, and the drawings they produced still hang beside the control desk.

The district also runs a small laboratory, staffed by two chemists and a rotating group of interns. Bench space is limited, so most samples wait in a refrigerator until the morning run. Results are logged against the intake readings, and any anomaly is flagged for the shift supervisor. Emergency generators sit in a separate building on higher ground and are tested under load on the first Tuesday of each month. The crew rotates roughly four hundred preventive tasks through the year, from lubricating a single bearing to repainting the clarifier weirs.

Public tours run on Saturday mornings between April and October. Visitors gather in the lobby, watch a short safety video, and then follow a guide along a raised walkway above the filter beds. The walkway is narrow and slippery in wet weather, so the district limits each group to twelve people and requires closed-toe shoes. Photography is allowed everywhere except the chlorine storage area, where signs in three languages warn of the hazard.
